This is Dave, and Dave presses every button he meets, usually more than once.
This morning, the walk button got eleven presses.
The lift's door-close got jabbed.
The thermostat went down two degrees.
Three buttons. Three wins.
Dave keeps score, and he's undefeated.
But in two thousand four, New York admitted that more than two thousand five hundred of its walk buttons did nothing.
Not broken. Disconnected, under a sign that still said push button.
So why is the world full of buttons that do nothing?
And why can't Dave stop pressing them?
Dave's morning had three buttons.
One of them was lying to him,
one was working for somebody else,
and one was working on Dave the whole time.
Start with the button Dave pressed eleven times.
New York's push-button signals go back to about nineteen sixty-four.
They sat where a quiet side street met a busy avenue.
The avenue stayed green until a car rolled up,
or someone on foot pressed the button.
Then the city filled with cars,
and computers took over, timing the lights along whole avenues at once.
Side streets got so busy that cars tripped the lights anyway,
and the buttons got in the way of the computer's plan.
So by the late nineteen eighties, most of them had been quietly switched off.
By two thousand four, that was more than two thousand five hundred buttons out of three thousand two hundred and fifty.
The Times called them mechanical placebos.
Nobody took them down, though.
Removing them would have cost about a million dollars,
and as one city official put it,
There's no harm in having it at the locations.
The sign on the pole gave two instructions.
Push button. Wait for walk signal.
Only the second one was doing anything.
The Times also met a four-year-old in Brooklyn, pressing away while his babysitter explained it never works.
Asked why he kept going, he said, because it's fun.
By twenty sixteen, the city told the Times it had a hundred and twenty working ones left.
And in twenty ten, ABC News checked crossings in Austin, Gainesville and Syracuse,
and found one button that worked.
But that's just America.
In twenty thirteen, the BBC timed a busy crossing on Regent Street in London.
Press the button, a hundred and five seconds.
Don't press it, a hundred and five seconds.
Transport for London said that one only listens between midnight and seven in the morning.
To be fair, London says most of its junction buttons do work,
and at a crossing away from any junction, the button really stops the cars.
Britain's newer Puffin crossings even have a sensor watching the kerb.
Press the button and wander off, and it's meant to cancel your request.
Finally, a button that checks you meant it.
Then researchers working for the Department for Transport inspected seventy-two Puffin crossings.
Only eleven had the cancel feature working.
So a walk button depends on the city, the junction and the hour.
Dave's eleven presses were a lottery ticket.
Next, the lift, where Dave jabbed door-close until the doors gave in.
In nineteen ninety, America passed the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Under its rules, lift doors must stay open at least three seconds,
and longer when someone is walking over from the call button.
The door-close button isn't allowed to cut that short.
And many lifts are set to close at about the minimum anyway,
so there's nothing left for the button to shorten.
The head of the elevator industry's trade group told the New York Times,
The riding public would not be able to make those doors close any faster.
So why does it feel like it works?
Drexel psychologist John Kounios pointed out that the doors always close eventually.
If the door never closed, we would stop pressing the button.
Dave pressed, the door closed,
and his brain filed it as a win.
But here's the part nobody tells Dave.
The door-close button isn't fake.
In a fire, a firefighter turns a key,
and from then on, the doors close only while someone holds that button down.
Let go too early, and they open again.
So it was never really Dave's button.
It belongs to the fire department, and Dave is allowed to borrow it.
Which leaves the thermostat, the one button Dave is truly proud of.
In two thousand three, a trade magazine called Air Conditioning, Heating and Refrigeration News asked its readers a quiet question.
Had they ever installed a dummy thermostat, wired to nothing?
Seventy people answered, and fifty-one said yes.
It was an informal online poll, so it isn't every office on Earth.
It might be Dave's, though.
One reader in Colorado wrote in about a thermostat that controlled nothing at all.
People felt better, he said,
and service calls fell by over seventy-five percent.
The fake thermostat fixed the complaints.
It just never touched the temperature.
Which raises a strange question.
If the room didn't change, why did the people in it feel better?
In nineteen seventy-five, psychologist Ellen Langer sold one-dollar lottery tickets to office workers.
Each ticket was a card with a football player on it.
Some people picked their own card, and others were simply handed one.
Just before the draw, she asked what price they'd sell their ticket back for.
Handed a ticket? About two dollars.
Picked it yourself? Almost nine.
Same odds. Same dollar. The only difference was the feeling of having chosen.
Langer called it the illusion of control,
acting as if you can steer something that's pure chance.
Dave's walk button was the same thing,
a lottery ticket he chose eleven times in a row.
So that settles it, right? Well, not quite.
In twenty twenty-one, a team at Wharton ran seventeen experiments with more than ten thousand people.
Choosing your own ticket mostly didn't make people feel any luckier.
One explanation they offer:
Langer's choosers may simply have liked their football player.
So the illusion of control might be partly an illusion. Fair.
Maybe fake buttons don't even fool us.
Maybe Dave is just a man who enjoys pressing plastic.
But around nineteen seventy, psychologists David Glass and Jerome Singer tested a different kind of button.
First, they recorded a terrible soundtrack.
Two people speaking Spanish, one speaking Armenian,
a mimeograph copier, a calculator and a typewriter, all at once.
They played it in random bursts at about a hundred and eight decibels,
while volunteers tried to work through tasks.
Some volunteers got a button on the side of their chair, and an instruction.
You can terminate the noise by pressing the button. But we'd prefer you not do it.
Almost nobody pressed it.
They heard the same noise, just as loud, for just as long.
Afterwards, everyone got puzzles, some of them secretly impossible,
and pages of text full of errors to find.
The people with no button gave up on the puzzles sooner, and missed more of the errors.
The people with a button they never used kept going,
and did about as well as people who could really switch the noise off.
The button didn't change the noise.
It changed what the noise did to them.
These are lab studies from more than fifty years ago, so hold them loosely,
but they do explain Colorado.
The dummy thermostat didn't cool the room.
It cooled the complaints.
So why is the world full of buttons that do nothing?
Partly because taking them out costs money.
And partly because they never stopped working.
They just work on the person, not the machine.
That doesn't make every fake button fine.
New York, under a court order from twenty twenty-one,
is putting new buttons at ten thousand crossings by twenty thirty-one.
These ones talk and vibrate, so someone who is blind knows when it's time to walk.
A button that tells the truth beats one that only feels good.
The next morning, Dave is back at the crossing, and he knows everything now.
He knows the walk button might be disconnected,
that door-close belongs to the fire department,
and that his thermostat may be wired to nothing.
He presses all three anyway.
Dave updates his scoreboard. Buttons that worked on the machine, maybe one.
Buttons that worked on Dave, all three.
Most buttons in your life do exactly what they say.
A few only work on you.
And the button that matters
is the one you think you have.
